title: Whose is it?
goal: Express possession with the endings -ae and -i, use the possessives meus and tuus correctly, and name the members of a Roman family.
bekal: ask *cuius est?* and answer with the "of" form
read a noun's dictionary form and know why it always lists two forms
put *meus, tua, nostrum* on the right thing — the thing owned, not the owner

dialogs.title: Colloquium — Anulus in horto
dialogs.intro: Iulia finds a ring in the garden. The whole household tries to guess who owns it.

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.id: Look, a ring! Whose ring is this?

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.text: Meus non est. Fortasse anulus Sexti est.
lines.id: It's not mine. Maybe it's Sextus's ring.
lines.literal: mine not is-it. perhaps ring Sextus-of is-it.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.id: Sextus is always walking around here.

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.text: Fortasse. Sed anulus feminae est, non viri.
lines.id: Maybe. But it's a woman's ring, not a man's.
lines.literal: perhaps. but ring woman-of is-it, not man-of.

lines.speaker: Cornelia:
lines.id: What are you shouting about, children?

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.id: Look, a ring, Mom! Is it yours?

lines.speaker: Cornelia:
lines.text: Ita, meus est! Anulus aviae meae est.
lines.id: Yes, it's mine! It's my grandmother's ring.
lines.literal: yes, mine is-it! ring grandmother-of my-of is-it.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.id: Grandmother's ring? Then it's really old!

lines.speaker: Cornelia:
lines.text: Ita. Gratias, liberi. Filia bona et filius bonus estis.
lines.id: Yes. Thank you, children. You're a good daughter and a good son.
lines.literal: yes. thanks, children-pl-call. daughter good-fem and son good-masc are-you-pl.

notes: **Cuius est? — "whose is it?"** This is the "of" form of *quis*. The answer uses the "of" form too: *Corneliae est* ("it's Cornelia's"), *Sexti est* ("it's Sextus's"), *viri est* ("it's the man's"). Notice that Latin needs no word for "of" or no *'s* at all — the ending carries that meaning.

**Anulus feminae, non viri.** Two words in one line show two groups at once: *femina* becomes *feminae*, *vir* becomes *viri*. Dictionaries use this "of" form to mark a word's group, which is why every noun is always listed twice: *femina, feminae* and *vir, viri*.

**Anulus aviae meae — two "of" endings in a row.** *Aviae* means "of grandmother", and *meae* matches *aviae*, not *anulus*. A possessive always follows the word it belongs to. The translation: "my grandmother's ring".

**Liberi means "children", not "free people".** It's the plural of *liber* ("free" — think *liberty*) used as a noun: in a Roman household, the children were the free people in it — as opposed to those who were enslaved. It's one of those words that carries a bitter history; this course uses it as it is.

blocks.text: The "of" form — called the genitive — expresses possession, origin and relationship. It translates English "of" and *'s*.

rows: ianua **scholae** — the door of the school
epistula **amici** — a letter from a friend

blocks.text: Words in *-us* and neuter words in *-um* share the same "of" form: *-i*. Words in *-er* like *magister* and *liber* drop their *e*: *magistri*, *libri*, *agri* — except *puer*, which keeps it: *pueri*. There are few words like this, and the dictionary always tells you.

blocks.title: Why the dictionary lists two forms
items: A Latin noun's dictionary form always has two parts: *puella, puellae* — the subject form and the "of" form. The second one tells you its group.
Ends in *-ae* → 1st declension. Ends in *-i* → 2nd declension. Ends in *-is* → 3rd declension (Unit 10). Ends in *-us* → 4th declension, ends in *-ei* → 5th declension (Unit 17).
So always learn nouns in pairs. *Hortus, horti* sticks much better than *hortus* alone, and once you know it, you can build all the other forms yourself.

blocks.text: Latin possessives behave like ordinary adjectives: they change outfits to match **the thing owned**, not the owner. English *his* and *her* follow the owner, so this often confuses learners at first.

head: Sentence
Translation
Why that form
rows: *amica* is feminine → *mea*, even though Marcus is male
*liber* is masculine → *meus*, even though Lydia is female

blocks.text: A possessive can stand before or after its noun. *Amicus meus* is the normal order; *meus amicus* sounds emphatic: "**my** friend, not yours". When calling someone, though, the possessive almost always comes first: *mi fili* ("my son") — and note *mi*, the irregular calling form of *meus*.

Some family words belong to the third declension, which you'll learn in Unit 10. For now just memorize them; the middle column shows the "of" form, which you can already use. Plenty of English cousins here: *paternal, maternal, filial, fraternal, sorority, marital*.

blocks.title: Familia doesn't mean "family"
items: In Latin, *familia* covers **the whole household**: father, mother, children, relatives living with them, and the enslaved people in it. It's closer to "household" than to "nuclear family".
The head of the household is the *pater familias* — note the old "of" form *familias*, not *familiae*. The phrase froze in an older age and was never updated.
*Domus* means a house as the family's home, while *villa* is a farmhouse outside town, and *insula* is a multi-story apartment block where most people in Rome actually lived.
